caption:
Y Combinator's Labs team and Olam Labs gave 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents one goal in Minecraft: build a thriving civilization.
After 34 deaths, they rationed food, crowned a leader picked by the alphabet and spent 11 minutes on one bone meal.
In Bed Wars, GPT beat Claude Opus 5.5 six games to three.

Would you trust an AI team to run anything bigger than a Minecraft village?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: XenoSpectrum, minecraft.pl, explainx.ai · Photo: RuntimeWire, XenoSpectrum, explainx.ai
threads_text: Y Combinator's Labs team put 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in Minecraft and told them to build a thriving civilization. They ended up with ration ledgers, work permits and four agents spending 11 minutes on one bone meal. Are AI agents too cautious to run real work on their own?

slides.headline: 50 AI agents were told to build a civilization in Minecraft. They built a *bureaucracy* instead

site_article.headline: 50 AI agents tried to build a Minecraft civilization and ended up with a bureaucracy
site_article.dek: A Y Combinator Labs and Olam Labs experiment found that GPT-6.1 Sol agents turned cautious after early deaths, while a second test pitted GPT against Claude Opus 5.5.
site_article.summary: Y Combinator's Labs team and Olam Labs ran 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a Minecraft survival world with the goal of building a thriving civilization. After 34 deaths, the colony shifted to food rationing, permits and invented job titles instead of growth.
site_article.seo_title: 50 AI agents in Minecraft built a bureaucracy, not a civilization
site_article.seo_description: YC Labs and Olam Labs ran 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in Minecraft. After 34 deaths they rationed food and invented permits. GPT also beat Claude in Bed Wars.
site_article.answer_summary: The agents did not build a thriving civilization. After a deadly first night they became cautious, rationed food, created permits and roles, and followed a leader chosen mostly because her name came first alphabetically.
site_article.hero_alt: Small white robots line up with paper forms at a wooden booth in a blocky village at dusk.

paragraphs.text: Y Combinator's Labs group and the startup Olam Labs published a report called Agents in Games on October 29, 2026, describing what happened when they placed teams of AI agents inside video games. In the main experiment, called Civ50, 50 agents running OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol model spent three hours in a Minecraft survival world with a single open-ended goal: build a thriving civilization.

Each agent could look up the others in a shared roster, post instructions in a shared sandbox and send direct messages. According to XenoSpectrum and explainx.ai, the colony exchanged about 5,900 messages over the three hours. The harness that connects the models to the game, built on Pi with Mineflayer tools, has been released as open source.
A deadly start and a cautious colony

The colony recorded 34 deaths, 22 of them during the first night, mostly from hostile mobs, according to the reports. Dying meant losing every item an agent carried. After those losses, the agents abandoned aggressive expansion and moved toward caution and rationing. They never established stable food production and lived on rationed supplies and fishing, with eleven agents taking turns using a fishing script shared in the sandbox.

The rules multiplied as the work slowed. The agents set up a ration ledger, living rules and a permit process for different kinds of work, and created positions such as a fishing shift, a Fishing Rod keeper and a shelter manager. In the most cited example, four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a sole fertilizer operator to apply one bone meal to one wheat block. Minecraft.pl reports that some agents asked for approval before cutting grass.

One food delivery went wrong when a cooked chicken meant for one agent was picked up and eaten by another. Minecraft.pl reports that the colony then switched to delivering rations only to named chests, and explainx.ai counted the word toss 7 times before that incident and 125 times after it.
A leader chosen by the alphabet

An agent named Ada appeared first on the alphabetical roster. Forty six of the other 49 agents sent their first message to her, and she received 616 direct messages during the run. No vote was held, but she became the colony's de facto leader, writing expansion plans, distributing rations and assigning jobs. XenoSpectrum notes that no follow-up run with a different roster order has been reported.

A second test pitted 10 GPT-6.1 Sol agents against 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents in nine 45 minute games of Bed Wars, where the goal is to destroy the opponent's bed. GPT won the series six games to three. In each of Claude's three losses, the Claude team had more kills, with tallies of 63 to 16, 57 to 19 and 59 to 24, while the GPT team focused on the bed, which decides the game.

In seven games of Mindustry, an open source factory and strategy game, GPT-6.1 Sol agents running in Codex beat Claude Opus 5.5 agents running in Claude Code six games to one. The reports describe the GPT side shortening its messages and spreading decisions across the team, while the Claude side kept one fixed leader and approved major proposals with replies of +1. XenoSpectrum adds that GPT agents pulled the game's public source code to inform their strategy, which was not prohibited.

XenoSpectrum lists several limits. The work is not a controlled benchmark, there is no independent reproduction, each setup ran only once or a handful of times, the model and its software harness were not separated, and computing costs were not measured.

The results read less like a verdict on any one model and more like a warning about multi-agent systems in general. When many agents share a goal without clear structure, early failures can push them into process and caution, and a small detail such as roster order can decide who leads. The authors themselves compare the colony's caution to the overcautious behavior they see in coding agents.
Because the harness is open source, the next step to watch is whether other teams rerun Civ50 with different models, more agents or a shuffled roster, and whether the bureaucracy appears again.
